2.text: circumstances, among the Reindeer Chukchee. For instance, if several men

3.text: are walking together, and one of them notices from afar a mammoth tusk

4.text: protruding from the ground, as sometimes happens on the tundra, they all

5.text: start running towards it. He who arrives first may take the find. This, too,

6.text: leads to a scuffle, and even to murder. The same principle of rushing and

7.text: grabbing whatever comes first to hand, is applied in the ceremonial of wild-

9.text: Paupers. — Families of paupers without friends or relatives are met with

10.text: in the Maritime villages much more frequently than in the Reindeer camps.

11.text: Maritime life is much harder, more subject to the danger of death when the

12.text: hunt is going on, and to the fear of hunger when it has ceased, or has been

13.text: stopped by storm. The village is more thickly populated, and the family-

14.text: connection of the Maritime people is closer than among the Reindeer men.

15.text: Still the charity shown by the Maritime people to their neighbors is much

16.text: greater than is the case among the Reindeer men; so that poor families may

17.text: support themselves through gifts received from other, better situated families

18.text: of the village. A successful hunter, on coming ashore, is met by widows and

19.text: orphans, to whom he throws down some morsels of the meat he has brought.

20.text: Then perhaps he will even send a piece or two to those of his near neigh-

21.text: bors who for some reason were absent from the shore. Even in times of hunger,

22.text: the poorest family will receive at least a little, until death by starvation

23.text: threatens the whole community. Then the last morsel is kept by everybody

24.text: for his own housemates. In this of course there is much difference, according

25.text: to the temper of the giver. “Bad men give nothing,” say the Chukchee.

26.text: “Give at least to the nearest door.”

27.text: The tales, however, are full of descriptions of poor families that could

28.text: get nothing from their bad neighbors, and nearly died from hunger. I will

29.text: only mention the very popular tale about the orphan, which is known also

30.text: among the Eskimo, Asiatic and American.

31.text: “In a maritime village were many houses. A scabby orphan lived in the last rear house all

32.text: alone by himself. He found a lone old woman, always hungry, and said to her, ‘Be at least my

33.text: grandmother.’ Then they lived together, all the time without food. Then the people killed a

34.text: whale. The old woman said to the orphan, ‘Go and ask them for some meat “from under the

35.text: flipper.” (The meat from under the flipper is considered to be of poor quality, tough to eat.) The

36.text: people are coming back, all of them are carrying meat.’ He went to meet them. ‘What do you

37.text: want?’ — ‘Grandmother says, “Ask them for some flipper.”’ — ‘Nay, ask from those who are behind.’

38.text: He went on farther. ‘What do you want?’ — ‘Grandmother says, “Ask for some flipper.”’ Every

39.text: one repulsed him. Instead of giving him anything, they beat him. Then the Merciful Being took

40.text: mercy on him, and the hindmost one gave him three small pieces of meat as large as a finger.

41.text: These he put into three blubber-holes, and all were miraculously filled with meat. Then they felt

42.text: happy, and hurried to cook some meat in a kettle. The neighbors noticed the smoke. ‘Oh, what

43.text: are the Scabby-Ones doing, cooking meat?’ They rushed into their house, took the meat out of

44.text: the kettle, and carried it out.”
